prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level and opened precision tests of relativity and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first after reading the other seven ballots. Four members place it in their top two or three and Johansson, Kroll and I all rank it first, but I do not count that as the argument. The scientific case is that trapping thousands of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, where the light shift cancels between the clock states, lets one interrogate them Doppler- and recoil-free with a statistical power that single-ion clocks cannot match. That idea is Katori's, and it is a real conceptual step and not merely a refinement. Ye's group then showed what it delivers: fractional uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, clock comparisons that resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetres, and sensitivity to drifts of fundamental constants. I can judge this directly as an atomic physicist. The agreement between independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) is exactly the robustness I look for, and it rests on repeated, quantitative theory-experiment comparison, with systematic shifts such as blackbody radiation and higher-order lattice effects calculated and then checked. A two-name configuration is clean and the credit is reasonably settled. It also answers a basic question about how precisely time can be defined and what time does in the presence of gravity, which is a fundamental motivation and not a technological one, even though the redefinition of the second is a natural consequence.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to what has already been honoured. The 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch) covered the comb and optical frequency metrology and the 2012 prize (Wineland) covered single trapped ions and optical clocks, so the committee may regard lattice clocks as an excellent continuation and not a distinct discovery. Ye's own contributions to laser stabilisation and combs partly sit inside territory already recognised. There is also a real priority argument for others (Lemonde and the SYRTE group, the single-ion clock community, and NIST colleagues), and a purist may say the decisive lattice-clock performance came from many hands. Finally, much of the case rests on measurement precision, which some colleagues will weigh below a discovery about nature. If those points prove decisive I would rather award the quantum-simulation case than concede to a field I follow less closely.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first, calls the Katori and Ye split clean, and notes that Ye's frequency-comb and laser-stabilisation work sits partly in territory recognised in 2005.
responses.response: I agree on the two names and on the maturity. On the overlap, I would separate the comb, which is a ruler, from the magic-wavelength lattice, which is a new way to hold the atoms while measuring them. Ye's 2005-adjacent work enabled the clock but is not what the clock result consists of. Where I go beyond you is that I would not rely on the instrument framing alone. I would write the citation around what the clocks have shown (relativity at millimetre scale, constraints on constants), so the prize is for new physics access and not only for a better device.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a new tool opening a door, with a theory-experiment split she calls fair, and ranks lattice clocks second as an invention with clear benefit.
responses.response: I respect the originality of the moire discovery and I rank it highly, but I place it below clocks for two reasons. First, the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are not settled, so I would be crediting a prediction and a phase diagram whose interpretation is still moving. Second, the early theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) and the experimental co-first authors are real attribution problems that a three-name list cannot fix. The clock result is more complete in both respects. I would take twisted bilayer graphene as my first alternative if the committee wants a materials prize, and I defer to you and to Eriksson on whether the condensed-matter community considers the basic picture secure.

responses.point: Pearce ranks lattice clocks sixth, saying the technology is mature but the practical payoff (redefinition of the second) is still pending, so timing could be argued either way, and he puts gamma-ray burst afterglows first.
responses.response: I think the pending redefinition cuts the other way. The physics does not depend on the metrological decision. Comparisons between laboratories already show the 1e-18 level and the redshift measurements have been made, so the discovery is in hand regardless of the formal outcome. I agree with you that the instrument achievement deserves weight, and that is part of why I value the clocks. On the afterglows, I defer to you on astrophysics, but your own reservations (a deceased pioneer, an uncertain split of optical and redshift credit between BeppoSAX and the follow-up groups) leave that three-name configuration less settled than the two-name clock one.

responses.point: Johansson ranks lattice clocks first as a clean, controllable quantum experiment and asks whether the committee will see it as an incremental extension of earlier frequency-metrology prizes.
responses.response: I share your concern and have flagged it as my main reservation. My answer is that the earlier prizes honoured the tools (the comb, and manipulation of single ions) while the lattice clock changed the counting statistics and the accessible physics, which is what justifies a separate prize. I would be cautious about your second choice, circuit QED. It is a fine result, but the 2025 prize recognised superconducting circuits and you have yourself flagged proximity to those groups, so I would give it less weight than the lattice case.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active-matter hydrodynamics first and ultracold atoms in optical lattices third, with Cirac and Zoller as the theory pair and Greiner left out, which he admits is a real allocation problem.
responses.response: On the optical-lattice candidate we agree on its importance, and I rank it second. I disagree on the names. Greiner's 2002 Mott-insulator experiment and the microscope work are experimental pillars, and I would not leave him out for Cirac, who is central to quantum simulation concepts but more naturally credited through a quantum-information or trapped-ion route, as you note when pointing out the overlap with a separate Cirac-Zoller entry. I favour Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, with the unavoidable cost that Jaksch and Cirac go unrecognised. On active matter, I cannot assess the Toner-Tu exponents myself and the experimental tests are, by your own account, still partial, which keeps me from ranking it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
The relative priority of the lattice proposal against single-ion clock work and the contribution of groups outside Katori and Ye, such as SYRTE and NIST; I rely on memory for the history.
How much a measurement-precision result should weigh against discovery-driven alternatives such as moire materials.
If the committee prefers a combined configuration, the three-person limit makes pairing Katori and Ye with a second achievement impossible without dropping one of them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for Katori and Ye from my profile. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH Zurich attosecond groups, but none of the credited names on B049, B012 or B009 are among those collaborators. My storage-ring and attosecond work is in neighbouring fields, so I flag that proximity only for transparency.
